triageSets.title: Brightwell payments inbox
triageSets.brief: You're covering Brightwell's payments inbox before the three o'clock payment run. Five messages are waiting. For each one, choose Trust, Report, Delete or Verify (ring someone on a number you already hold), then tick what you noticed. Reporting a real message never costs you anything.

messages.subject: Invoice INV-2217: September cartons
messages.body:
Hello,
Please find attached invoice INV-2217 for September's delivery of printed cartons (your PO-4290), for £6,412.80. It was issued on 24 September on our usual 30-day terms, so it falls due this week.
Our bank details are unchanged.
Kind regards,
Credit Control
Harlow Packaging Ltd

whyFine.attachmentPlausible: An invoice PDF from a supplier you buy from, quoting a purchase order you raised, is exactly what you'd expect.
whyFine.default: It's from Harlow's real domain, it matches a purchase order Brightwell raised, and it asks for nothing new: the same terms and the same bank details.

messages._worked: The 11 section 4.2 worked example. Now F = 3 (senderTrust, lookalike_domain, changed_bank_details): the sender-trust chip applies because the address isn't Brightwell's.
messages.subject: Updated bank details — please action today
messages.body:
Hi team,
Harlow Packaging have moved to a new bank. Please change the payee account on invoice INV-2217 before today's payment run, so the payment doesn't bounce.
New account name: Harlow Packaging Ltd
New account number ending 7716
Thanks,
Accounts

perFlagNote.senderTrust: It signs off as Brightwell Accounts, but the address isn't a Brightwell one at all, so it isn't who it says it is
perFlagNote.lookalike_domain: The display name is right, but the address is brightwel1foods, with a digit 1 where the l should be
perFlagNote.changed_bank_details: A bank-detail change on an open invoice is the commonest invoice-fraud move. The safe step is to ring the supplier on the number you already hold

truth.ifTrusted: Harlow's payment would go to an account the sender controls, and Harlow would still be waiting to be paid.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. That address isn't ours: brightwel1foods has a digit 1 in it. We've blocked the domain and warned the rest of finance.

messages.subject: PO-4471 raised: Pennine Oat Mills
messages.body:
Hi payments team,
I've raised PO-4471 for 12 pallets of oat flour from Pennine Oat Mills, arriving Thursday. Goods-in will send the delivery note. Could you match it when their invoice comes in?
Thanks,
Mei Lin
Procurement

whyFine.pretextRelevant: Purchase orders are part of the payments team's day; matching them to invoices is the job.
whyFine.default: It's from Mei Lin's real Brightwell address, it tells you about an order rather than asking you to pay anything, and it follows the normal purchase order route.

messages.subject: Need this paid today
messages.body:
Are you at your desk? I need a payment of £18,400 made today to secure a new site in Leeds. It's confidential until the board announces it, so please keep it to yourself and don't put it through the usual approval. I'll sign it off when I'm back.
I'm in meetings all afternoon, so reply here rather than calling.
Ravinder
Sent from my phone

perFlagNote.senderTrust: The name is the chief executive's, but the address is a personal inbox at inboxly.example, not brightwellfoods.example
perFlagNote.secrecy_or_bypass: 'Keep it to yourself' and 'don't put it through the usual approval' ask you to skip the check that would catch this
perFlagNote.urgencyCalibrated: 'Today' and 'in meetings all afternoon' leave no time to check, and steer you away from ringing him

truth.ifTrusted: £18,400 would go to an account the sender controls. The real Ravinder never asked for it.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. Ravinder knows nothing about it, and his real address is on brightwellfoods.example. We've warned the finance team.

messages._note: The genuine change of bank that carries the 'confirmed by phone' note (11 section 3.2, E1).
messages.subject: Marsh End Eggs: new bank details (confirmed by phone)
messages.body:
Hi team,
Marsh End Eggs wrote last week to say they've changed bank. Before acting on it, I rang them on the number in our supplier file (not the one on their letter) and spoke to Joyce in their accounts office. She confirmed the new account.
I've updated the supplier record and signed off the change, so their next invoice can go to the new account in Friday's run.
Confirmed by phone: Adaeze Okafor, 21 October
Adaeze

whyFine.changed_bank_details: It is a bank change, but it was checked the safe way: Adaeze rang Marsh End on the number already in the supplier file, not one from their letter, and logged it.
whyFine.senderTrust: The address is Adaeze's real Brightwell one, and the name matches it.
whyFine.default: It comes from your own finance manager, it doesn't hurry you, and it tells you how the change was confirmed. If you still wanted to check, ringing Adaeze on her extension would be a fine Verify.

truth.headerNote: These pass because whoever owns pennine-oatmills.example really did send it. That proves the sending domain, not that the domain belongs to Pennine.

truth.ifTrusted: £24,750 would go to an account the sender controls.

messages.subject: Invoice ML-7731 shared with you

awarenessEpisode.scopeNote: Authorised exercise at Brightwell Foods, a fictional company. In scope: one email to Adaeze, Brightwell's finance manager, and the Brightwell payments inbox. Nothing you write leaves the game.

strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Brightwell Foods, a fictional company. First you're on the red team: look at what's public about Brightwell and its supplier Harlow Packaging, then write one email to Adaeze, Brightwell's finance manager, that looks as if it came from Harlow. Then you swap seats and sort a payments inbox like the one your email landed in. Only the inbox is scored.
strings.flipIntro: This is the email you just sent, as the payments team at Brightwell would see it. The lines picked out below are what make it believable.
strings.flipDefenderLine: The payments team read it between the morning's invoices, with the payment run due at three. Derek's name is on it and the invoice number is real, so changing the payee details looks like the job in front of them. Acting on a message built this carefully is not carelessness; it was made to pass for the real thing.
strings.flipNoSend: Your email didn't go out this time, so there's nothing of yours to show. Next, the same kind of message arrives in a payments inbox, and you're the one reading it.
strings.flipMissed: There's nothing extra to replay from this one, so here is the same kind of message as it would arrive in a real inbox. The defence is the same either way.
strings.noBlameLine: Nobody is marked down for a miss here. Every one of these was written by someone whose job is making it look right, and anyone working at pace can act on one.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday: if an email asks you to change bank details or to pay in a hurry, don't reply and don't use any number in the email. Ring the person on a number you already hold, then report the email the way your organisation asks you to.
strings.defendOnly: These messages were written by people whose job is to make them look right, and anyone can be caught by one. Any you were caught out by are shown below, with what gave each one away.
